source_document.body:
Harley-Davidson-born electric motorcycle maker LiveWire has issued a troubling warning about its financial future, announcing that it has substantial doubt about its ability to continue operating as a going concern. The news sent LiveWire’s stock plunging more than 40% on Thursday morning as the company withdrew its full-year financial guidance.
The announcement comes despite some signs of improving sales, with LiveWire reporting a 38% increase in third-quarter revenue to $7.9 million and a 21% rise in motorcycle unit sales. However, the company continues to burn through cash, reporting a net loss of $18.6 million for the quarter.
LiveWire’s cash reserves have also dwindled significantly, falling from $82.8 million at the end of 2025 to just $39.9 million as of September 30, 2026.
The company has now formed a special restructuring committee to explore potential financing arrangements, strategic partnerships, investments, or even a sale. It also withdrew its previous guidance projecting a $70 million to $80 million operating loss for 2026.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
The financial warning comes at a particularly pivotal moment for LiveWire, which is preparing to launch its most affordable electric motorcycles yet.
The upcoming LiveWire S4 Honcho series represents a major departure from the company’s existing premium electric motorcycles, offering smaller, lighter, and significantly more affordable models designed to attract a much broader audience of riders with a starting price below US $5,000.
LiveWire S4 Honcho Street electric motorcycle
The lower prices could dramatically increase LiveWire’s sales volumes, especially as the company attempts to move beyond the relatively small market for high-dollar electric motorcycles. The Honcho lineup is also expected to help lower the barrier to entry for new riders, with approachable electric motorcycles that eliminate the complexity of clutch and gear shifting.
LiveWire is also preparing to showcase its latest developments at EICMA in Milan next week , where it is expected to display new models and further expand its upcoming electric motorcycle lineup.
Whether those new motorcycles can arrive quickly enough to turn around the company’s financial situation remains to be seen.
Electrek’s Take
This is genuinely sad news to see. If there’s any legacy motorcycle manufacturer that deserves to succeed in the electric motorcycle space, it’s Harley-Davidson.
Make all the jokes you want about old dudes in leather jackets riding around on loud, chrome-covered motorcycles. But the fact is that Harley-Davidson was taking electric motorcycles seriously when most other major motorcycle manufacturers were still pretending they didn’t exist.
Harley-Davidson didn’t just dip its toes into electric motorcycles. It dove in headfirst, developing the original LiveWire electric motorcycle well over a decade ago and eventually bringing a highly acclaimed production bike to market in 2019. That’s right, Harley-Davidson had a legitimately impressive electric motorcycle on the road before COVID was even a thing. Meanwhile, most of its legacy competitors are only now starting to roll out their first serious electric offerings.
And that’s what makes this so frustrating. Harley-Davidson did the hard part. It invested early, developed excellent technology, received rave reviews, and proved that electric motorcycles could be thrilling, premium machines. But building great motorcycles and building a profitable electric motorcycle business have turned out to be two very different challenges.
The timing is especially unfortunate because I genuinely believe LiveWire’s upcoming S4 Honcho series could be exactly what the company needs. These smaller, significantly more affordable electric motorcycles could finally open LiveWire up to a younger audience that doesn’t have $15,000 to drop on a flagship motorcycle but still wants something fun, stylish, and electric for $5,000.
In many ways, that audience seems like a much more natural fit for LiveWire’s branding and ethos than the premium motorcycle market it has been chasing for years.
I really hope LiveWire can find what it needs to get through this difficult period. After spending more than a decade helping drag the legacy motorcycle industry kicking and screaming into the electric age, it would be a real shame to see the company stumble just as its most promising chapter might be about to begin.

The ALSO TM-B is one of the most technologically interesting new e-bikes to hit the road in years, largely because it does away with one of the most fundamental parts of a bicycle: the mechanical connection between the pedals and rear wheel. With only copper wires connecting the pedals to the rear wheel, the TM-B is one of the most revolutionary new e-bikes in years.
But that raises an obvious question. What happens when the battery dies?
One early Launch Edition owner, Aaron Draczynski, decided to find out by deliberately running his TM-B down toward empty to see whether ALSO’s drive-by-wire system would leave him stranded.
He shared the experience on YouTube, discovering that the answer is surprisingly complicated – and involves something called “Infinite Turtle Mode.”
Advertisement - scroll for more content
First, the TM-B slowly takes away your power
Unlike a conventional e-bike, where the rider’s pedaling mechanically turns the rear wheel through a chain or belt, the ALSO TM-B uses a pedal-by-wire drivetrain. Pedaling generates electricity, while the rear wheel is driven electrically.
That arrangement enables all sorts of interesting features, including electronically simulated gearing and the Launch Edition’s massive Level 10 boost mode, which can multiply rider input by up to 10 times.
But it also means there’s no traditional drivetrain to fall back on when the battery runs out.
Fortunately, the bike doesn’t simply go from full power to dead.
The owner began his experiment at 31% charge and quickly watched the bike progressively restrict its maximum assist as the battery drained closer to empty. From 23% to 13%, the maximum boost dropped from Level 8 to Level 5 as it began conserving battery.
By 10% charge, the bike was limited to Level 4. At 8%, it dropped to Level 3, followed by Level 2 at 5%. Shortly afterward, only Level 1 remained. Then at 4% battery, conventional electric assistance disappeared entirely.
Interestingly, the normal electronic shifting of the bike’s simulated software gears continued to work through most of that process. But when the battery reached 4%, things changed as the bike started exhibiting issues. The first sign of trouble came when the bike began seemingly randomly shifting gears while in manual mode without the rider even touching the shifter. Several times per second, the bike seemed to want to shift itself between gears.
Keep in mind that the TM-B doesn’t have actual physical gears (and no chain or derailleur, for that matter), but instead simulates various gears using predefined software to make the rider feel like they are working more or less intensely to pedal the bike.
Image credit: Aaron Draczynski via https://www.youtube.com/@papermodelplane
Enter ‘Infinite Turtle Mode’
Once the TM-B reached its final low-battery state, an infinity symbol appeared on the display and the bike entered what the owner referred to as “Infinite Turtle Mode.”
Instead of using stored battery energy to provide meaningful assistance, the system effectively attempts to pass the rider’s pedaling energy through the electronic drivetrain to keep the rear wheel turning. It’s similar in concept to those old crank-powered flashlights, which, even with a dead storage battery, would still illuminate for as long as the owner cranked them.
And on flat ground, the owner reported that the infinite turtle mode apparently worked surprisingly well.
Draczynski described the experience as roughly equivalent to pedaling a normal bicycle in fourth gear. There was resistance at the pedals, and he could maintain a reasonable pace without feeling like he was simply spinning his legs uselessly.
Image credit: Aaron Draczynski
Then he reached a hill and found the limitation of that effectiveness. Even a slight incline transformed the experience, with the bike feeling more like it was permanently stuck in seventh or eighth gear. Getting home through his hilly neighborhood became, in his words, a “truly grueling ordeal.”
Manual shifting was also disabled in this mode, meaning there was no way to electronically select an easier virtual gear for climbing, since again, there aren’t any physical gears in the bike. Everything in the pedaling experience is software-simulated.
That’s an important limitation for a bike relying entirely on a drive-by-wire drivetrain. The infinite turtle mode might keep you moving with significant effort on level terrain, but it doesn’t turn a dead TM-B into a conventional bicycle, unless that conventional bicycle is being ridden through beach sand.
The low-power state apparently shuts down some other features as well. The owner could no longer lock or unlock the TM-B through ALSO’s smartphone app, though he did report the bike’s touchscreen controls continued working, and he guessed that the bike had shut down connectivity to conserve power for its key systems to operate.
Image credit: Aaron Draczynski
There’s another battery problem to watch
Perhaps more concerning than the low-battery riding experience was what happened when this particular TM-B was simply sitting in the owner’s garage.
Describing another scenario he encountered, Draczynski says he left the bike sitting unplugged in his garage at around 70% charge. The following evening, it had fallen to 40%, and a day later it was down to 18%.
When he returned the next morning, the TM-B displayed a “Bike issue detected” message followed by “Install battery to ride.”
There was just one problem: the battery was already installed.
Plugging in the charger didn’t initially help because the bike apparently couldn’t detect its own battery, and thus charging didn’t begin. Worse, the battery refused to eject using the normal ejection process, leaving the owner unable to remove it and charge it off of the bike.
Image credit: Aaron Draczynski
Ultimately, Draczynski used the physical reset button underneath the frame, which brought the system back to life. The bike recognized the battery again and began charging normally.
That degree of overnight battery drain obviously isn’t something we’d expect from a normal e-bike, so hopefully this was either an isolated software issue or something ALSO can address with an update. For his part, Draczynski suspects that the bike might be draining its battery so heavily at rest due to the lack of a cell signal in his garage. “I was quite surprised at the drop from day to day,” he explained on Reddit . “If I had to wager a guess, the bike might be searching for a cellular signal, but there’s no reception in my garage so it’s just draining the battery.”
But the experiment offers an interesting first real-world look at one of the biggest questions surrounding ALSO’s unusual drivetrain.
A normal e-bike with a dead battery becomes a heavy bicycle. The TM-B instead becomes something much stranger: an electricity-generating exercise machine that uses your legs to generate current, electronically sends that current through the bike, and then uses it to turn the rear wheel via the rear hub motor.
And based on this testing, it does in fact work. Just try not to be at the bottom of a hill when you find out for yourself.

2026 SEMA Show • Honda Racing Releases Its First-Ever In-House Made Parts for the Civic Type R and Integra Type S
Triple Black Corvette Restored to NCRS Standards, the Selling Price Is Obvious
27 photos
Photo: eBay seller capefear96terry
You won’t see many like this. A 1966 Chevrolet Corvette that has already been restored checks all the right boxes to impress the NCRS judges is trying to sell at a price that can hardly surprise anyone.
While the 1966 model year might not be as desirable as its predecessors - certainly not as desirable as the 1963 split-window coupe - this car is a rare triple-black configuration. It wears a beautiful black finish paired with a black cabin and a black top. It does look exquisite, and the restoration that was finished not long ago certainly made everything more eye-catching.
The car landed on eBay because it’s trying to find a new home. It’s now parked in the heated garage that’s been serving as shelter since the restoration was finished, and this is probably where it’ll continue to sleep until it leaves for a new garage.
Photo: eBay seller capefear96terry While the changes that took place in the engine lineup are probably the most notable on the 1966 Corvette, the thing I’ll always remember about this model year was the design of the backup lights. Chevrolet redesigned them and integrated them directly into the taillights for a reason that made perfect sense: backup lights were now standard on all Corvettes, so offering them outside the taillights no longer made sense.
Otherwise, yes, the engine lineup received one notable upgrade: a big-block - an actual big block - was now available. After going for a 396 in 1965, Chevrolet now launched a 427 that joined the lineup with two power configurations.
A 327 continued to be standard with 300 horsepower, while the L79 was the upgraded version of this engine with 350 horsepower. The L36 was the first big-block setup in the lineup, using a displacement of 427 cubic inches to produce 390 horsepower.
The L72 was the top configuration and was an upgraded version of the L36. It used a higher compression ratio - 11.0:1 versus 10.25:1 - and mechanical valve lifters versus hydraulic to produce 425 horsepower.
Photo: eBay seller capefear96terry The L72 wasn’t the rarest engine on the 1966 Corvette, despite being the most expensive at $312. This unit made its way to 5,528 Vettes, but fewer buyers - 5,116 - decided to pay less - $181.20 - for the upgrade to the 390-horsepower version.
Chevrolet ended the year with 27,720 Corvettes rolling off the assembly line, and the convertible was the more popular configuration with 17,762 units. The coupe accounted for 9,958 orders.
While this is a convertible, the triple black setup makes it significantly rarer. While I couldn’t find any production numbers - Chevrolet didn’t offer a breakdown by interior and top color - the documentation that sells with the car confirms this Corvette hasn’t been altered. It did leave the factory with this triple-black setup, and that’s precisely how it was restored and maintained.
The original build sheet indicates that the first buyer ordered the car in Tuxedo Black paired with the black trim and a black convertible top. He also paid extra for the side dual exhaust system, the PB AM/FM radio, and the 4-speed transmission.
The car was and still is powered by the 425-horsepower TurboJet engine. The engine received a complete refresh during the restoration, so everything is now in perfect shape. The car starts, runs, and drives beautifully, though it didn’t spend much time on the road after the restoration was finalized.
The car is “all matching numbers, including glass, carburetor, transmission, and rear,” the seller explains.
Photo: eBay seller capefear96terry At first glance, this Corvette has it all, and it’s hard to find a better convertible if you’re into this triple-black setup. Already restored and sporting the top engine you could get in 1966, this specimen will probably find a home eventually, though there’s no doubt this won’t happen overnight.
The reason is as simple as it could be: such a car is not affordable, and a high price means that finding the right person to pay for it could take a while.
The seller believes $150,000 is a fair price, but they also enabled the Make Offer option on eBay to allow further negotiations. You can click this button if you want the car but have another deal in mind, and you can start from here if you’re interested in this Corvette.
Photo: eBay seller capefear96terry I can’t stress enough how important it is to see the car in person before making an offer because not everything you see online also matches real life. A walkaround video would also come in handy, and photos taken during the restoration should help a potential buyer figure out if this Corvette received the top refresh advertised on eBay.
If you want to see it with your eyes, you’ll need to pack your bags for a trip all the way to Delray Beach, Florida. The listing will expire in 19 days, so you have enough time to convince your significant other that you need another classic Corvette and arrange an in-person inspection with the seller.
Via // eBay

New Android Auto Update Is Bad News for Notifications, Version 18.1 Doesn't Help
6 photos
Photo: Google
If you need more proof that updating to a new Android Auto version on release date is not a good idea, here’s a notification bug that seems to be plaguing unlucky users who installed a recent update.
It’s all happening on devices running Android 17 and seemingly an Android Auto version newer than 17.9.
Someone on the Google forums says Android Auto 17.9 itself introduced this problem, but I was running version 18.0 when I first noticed it.
Due to this glitch, notifications no longer have sound on Android Auto, so while you might see the pop-up appearing on the screen, no audio goes through the car’s speakers. Oddly, it looks like Android Auto is actually trying to play the notification sound, as it pauses the music to play the notification sound, but no alert goes through the speakers.
The issue doesn’t appear very widespread at the moment, but users claim this is very new and only introduced by an update shipped this week. They point to version 17.9 as the most recently-installed Android Auto build - which makes sense, considering the rollout of this version in the stable channel is now supposed to reach broad availability - but the same thing seems to be happening on the newer 18.0 build.
The first thing that I tried was clearing the cache and the data in Android Auto because this workaround sometimes deals with small glitches like this one. It didn’t, and the notification sounds are still muted for Android Auto apps. I installed Android Auto 18.1 beta manually to see if the problem still occurs, and everything went back to normal on the first run.
The bug returned after I turned off the engine and disconnected the phone from my car, so eventually, version 18.1 did not help and seems to be suffering from the same glitch. Once I removed all Android Auto updates and started from scratch, everything went back to normal, but the notification sound bug reappeared once I updated to the latest version.
I run Android Auto with a Google Pixel 10 Pro XL and a factory-installed head unit with wireless support.
The only fix that I found, at least until Google comes up with a fix, is to remove all updates and block the automatic installation of new versions through the Google Play Store. Unfortunately, this could lead to other problems, as sticking with an older version means that you’re not getting the latest fixes and improvements, so you could end up hitting other bugs that have already been resolved.
A Google Community Specialist has already requested additional bug data on Google’s forums, and if you’re also battling this error, make sure you drop a comment in that thread.

Magellan Discoverer Is the First Hybrid-Electric Polar Cruise Ship Built in South America
7 photos
Photo: Antarctica21
The newest ship ready to join the fleet of Antarctica21, a leading name in boutique, small-ship expeditions to the White Continent, is a pioneer for shipbuilding in the Americas. Magellan Discoverer marks a major milestone for the biggest shipyard in Chile, as South America’s first hybrid-electric expedition ship.
Asenav (Astilleros y Servicios Navales S.A.) announced the beginning of sea trials for Magellan Discoverer, an expedition cruise ship unlike any other built in the region. Cruise operator Antarctica21 commissioned it in 2023, based on the successful platform of Megallan Explorer, which was also built by Asenav and delivered in 2019.
The new Magellan Discoverer is, first of all, a rugged polar cruise ship with a reinforced hull and the ability to break through ice that’s 80 cm (2.6 feet) thick. Complete with a Polar Class PC6 rating and an IMO Tier III certification (International Maritime Organization’s classification for maximum emission levels permitted), this new-generation cruise ship is meant to provide safe, efficient travel to the White Continent, while also protecting wildlife and the environment.
According to Antarctica21, every system on board was specifically engineered to reduce environmental impact, so it’s not just about the hybrid-electric propulsion. The advanced anti-fouling system, for instance, prevents marine organism from getting attached to the hull, which in turn helps reduce drag, but without the toxic biocides used previously in cruising.
The ballast water management system uses treated seawater to maintain the stability of the ship, in line with current environmental regulations to prevent ecological disruption. The onboard waste management system also meets stringent IMO requirements. The integrated heat recovery system captures waste heat from the engine exhaust gases and then uses its onboard hotel systems, which reduces reliance on fuel-fired boilers to a great extent.
Some of these advanced features, including the reverse osmosis water system that converts seawater into freshwater, are also involved in keeping this long-range expedition ship autonomous during longer periods of time. As for the hybrid-electric propulsion system, it features two MAN main engines, the ABB hybrid DC grid (a modular platform that combines generator power with battery storage), and ABB Azipod propulsion.
The Corvus Energy Battery Storage System allows zero-emission operations in sensitive environments, as well as lower noise levels, and overall more flexible energy management. The Azipods ensure so-called 360-degree propulsion, which translates to better maneuverability, reduced underwater noise, and a lower impact on wildlife.
The 94-meter (308 feet) ship built to accommodate up to 96 passengers is set to enter service with Antarctica21 on December 15, this year. For the operator’s signature fly-cruise programs, where passengers avoid the challenging Drake Passage by flying straight to King George Island, where they embark on the ship, Magellan Discoverer will be limited to 88 guests.

This Tiny Device Brings Lossless Wireless Music Into Your Super-Old Car
9 photos
Photo: iFi
iFi has just unveiled a device that’s no bigger than your AirPods case and whose purpose is as simple as it could be: to transform the music experience in your ancient car in the easiest possible way. The UP Travel Max is essentially an adapter that can send and receive lossless audio via Bluetooth, and it can connect to pretty much anything that has an AUX input or a 3.5mm jack.
If you own an older car, let’s say a model year before 2015, you probably discovered the hard way that getting Android Auto and CarPlay isn’t, let’s say, affordable. A head unit upgrade is the most common advice, but these things obviously aren’t cheap.
They start at maybe $200 for the entry-level setups and can easily go over $1,000 for a premium head unit that has all the modern stuff.
If you’re lucky, your carmaker installed Bluetooth, letting you connect your smartphone to your vehicle to stream music to the cabin stereo system and talk to the phone, you know, without risking losing your driver’s license. If you’re not, you’re probably with an AUX connector that doesn’t do much, except let you connect your old-school MP3 player - seriously now, is anyone still using these things? - to listen to your favorite tunes.
That’s why iFi UP Travel Max is at least worth a look.
Photo: iFi I admit that iFi’s press release caught my attention with all the tech that it highlighted, beginning with CD-quality sound with aptX Lossless and LDAC. The company says the adapter uses a dedicated Qualcomm Bluetooth chip to handle the connection to whatever device you pair with it and a Cirrus Logic MasterHIFI Dac to handle the wireless signal.
“The result is a cleaner, more detailed sound, wherever you’re listening,” it says.
In plain English, this adapter can be both a transmitter and a receiver, but since we’re here because we’re obsessed with cars, let’s see what it can do in your car. Technically, it must be plugged into your AUX port, assuming you have an old stereo with such an input, and it lets you stream music from your phone via Bluetooth.
Photo: iFi You’ll be able to listen to your tunes directly through the car’s speakers, and iFi promises you’ll get CD-quality sound even if you stream wirelessly.
Before you ask, you can use whatever music app you want to listen to your music. Spotify, YouTube Music, Apple Music, a local media player- everything works as long as it runs on your phone because the adapter doesn’t care about what app you’re using as long as the audio comes through the Bluetooth connection.
The device uses Bluetooth 5.4, and when it switches to the transmitter role, it can send audio to multiple devices thanks to Auracast integration. You need to own Auracast-compatible headphones for this feature.
It sports a 400 mAh battery, and the parent company says this should be enough for approximately 10 hours of battery life. You can recharge the adapter using the USB-C cable, and considering most of us already have such cords in our cars, this shouldn’t be a major shortcoming, even if the battery doesn’t last as long as the manufacturer promises.
Photo: iFi This feature comes in handy specifically when you try to use wired devices with wireless headphones, and iFi highlights to specific scenarios. One of them is during your flights, where we typically get a headphone jack integrated into the headrest-mounted screens, and the other one is an old-school iPod.
Before I reveal the price, I can’t help but state the obvious thing: the concept isn’t new, and similar devices have been available for quite some time. Maybe not in the same premium form factor, but such products, offering similar capabilities and letting you turn an AUX port into a wireless receiver, can already be found on Amazon.
This UGREEN adapter does pretty much the same thing, coming with a headphone jack that you can plug into your vehicle’s AUX port to receive audio signals wirelessly via Bluetooth. Furthermore, it also offers LDAC and Bluetooth 6.0, and it doesn’t require any sophisticated configuration. You plug it in, pair it with your smartphone, and start streaming music as if you’re listening to music on Bluetooth headphones.
Photo: UGREEN The UGREEN adapter costs $18.99 on Amazon today, and you might be able to get it even cheaper shortly, considering Black Friday is just around the corner.
Obviously, there are plenty of other alternatives out there, some selling for as low as $10. They come from generic Chinese brands, though their reliability and audio quality might not be what you expect.
Otherwise, if money isn’t an issue and you’d rather pay a premium for iFi’s new UP Travel Max, be ready to spend $129. The box includes the adapter, one USB-C to USB-A adapter (for cars that still use the old USB design), one USB-C to USB-C cable, and the typical paperwork to get you started.
